title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview:

This document consolidates the serving runtime guidance used by Redwood Inference engineers: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes summary, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as a single reference for design decisions, performance debugging, and oncall procedures.

Sections in this page:
1) Architecture overview
2) Kernel scheduling design and heuristics
3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
4) Benchmarking suite and test recipes
5) Release notes & upgrade checklist (summary)
6) Known issues and mitigations
7) Runtime runbooks (incidents, scaling, rollbacks)
8) Team wiki pointers, ownership, and links

## 1) Architecture overview

Summary:
- Serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine providing low-latency token generation, multi-model hosting, KV cache management, and continuous batching.
- Design goals: predictable p95 latency, high throughput (tokens/sec), graceful degradation, and transparent performance telemetry.

Core components:
- Frontend API router: TLS-terminated, per-tenant authorization, rate-limiting, and initial request shaping. Owned by eng-platform.
- Request router & policy engine: makes routing decisions (latency/cost/region), selects model variant and fallback.
- Inference workers: GPU-backed processes (containerized) running the runtime binary. Handles token generation, KV cache, attention kernels, quantized paths.
- Batcher: groups compatible requests according to shape/seq_len/model to utilize matrix kernels efficiently.
- Cache service: prefix/KV cache (hot prefixes) with eviction policy and shared memory access for workers.
- Telemetry & metrics: per-request traces, token-level cost, kernel-level timings, memory pressure events.

Cross-cutting constraints and SLOs:
- P95 token generation latency target: 120ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens) for tier=standard in region=us-west-2.
- Uptime SLA for Dedicated pools: 99.9% (monthly).
- Alerting thresholds: GPU temperature > 85C, memory utilization > 92%, sustained queueing latency > 200ms.

## 2) Kernel scheduling design and heuristics

Goals: maximize GPU utilization while preserving latency SLOs and minimizing context-switch overhead.

Primary strategies:
- Work grouping: requests are partitioned into scheduling classes by model variant, dtype (fp16/int8), and sequence length bucket.
- Continuous batching: scheduler waits up to batch_wait_ms (configurable) to fill a batch but enforces a max_wait_ms to avoid tail latency.
- Kernel selection: per-model kernel table maps (model, dtype, seq_len) -> preferred kernel implementation. Fallback to generic kernel if optimized kernel unavailable.
- Preemption policy: short low-latency classes (LL) are prioritized over throughput classes (TP). Preemption is cooperative—running kernels are not interrupted but next dispatch favors LL class.

Scheduling parameters (example table):
| param | description | default | notes |
| batch_wait_ms | time to accumulate requests | 3 | tuned per region and service tier |
| max_batch_size | maximum requests per batch | 64 | dependent on GPU memory and kernel |
| preempt_threshold_ms | threshold before preemption favoring LL | 10 | if queueing > threshold, prefer LL |
| seq_len_buckets | bucket boundaries for batching | [32,128,512,2048] | helps choose kernels |

Heuristics for tuning:
- For models with long KV cache reuse (chat workloads), set larger batch_wait_ms to improve batching efficiency; ensure p95 remains under SLO.
- If memory pressure observed during large-batch synthetic benchmarks, reduce max_batch_size or use mixed-precision kernels.

## 3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to profile:
- Regression in latency/throughput observed in production or benchmarks.
- Kernel-level hotspots or GPU memory anomalies.
- New model onboarding or quantization rollout.

Quick checklist:
1. Gather baseline metrics: time-range traces (x-request-id), p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, GPU metrics (util, mem, temp).
2. Reproduce workload in perf cluster (use perf-runner, see benchmarking suite). Tag the run with run_id and commit.
3. Collect kernel-level traces: enable runtime kernel profiler (--profiler=kernel, sample_rate=1000).
4. CPU-side traces: enable thread and scheduling traces (perf, eBPF script in /ops/profiling).
5. Analyze hot kernels and memory spikes; map back to model layer (attention, matmul, softmax).
6. If kernel is generic, try an optimized kernel from kernel-table and re-run benchmark.
7. Validate user-visible metrics and SLOs. If fix is needed, open a PR and include perf artifacts.

Commands and example workflows:
- Start profiler on a worker:
  ./runtime --model-path /models/llama-3b-fp16 --profiler=kernel --prof-output /tmp/run123.kprof
- Collect host GPU counters (NVIDIA):
  sudo nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o TD -f /tmp/gpu_dmon.csv
- Run perf harness (perf-cluster):
  infra/perf-runner --config perf/configs/chat-128.json --run-id run123 --commit abcdef

Artifacts to attach to an incident or PR:
- kernel profiler output (.kprof), GPU counter csv, perf harness logs, representative request traces, model config (vocab, seq_len, dtype).

## 4) Benchmarking suite and test recipes

Purpose: provide reproducible, auditable performance baselines for model variants and runtime changes.

Benchmark types:
- Microbenchmarks: kernel-only math ops, memory copy bandwidth, KV cache hit/miss latency.
- Synthetic workloads: fixed prompt distributions to stress batcher and kernel selection.
- Replay workloads: sampled real traffic replay (anonymized) to validate end-to-end performance.

Example configs (perf/configs):
- chat-128.json: chat prefix distribution, 90% short-turn (<=64), 10% long-turn (<=512).
- embeddings-512.json: batching for embed-only requests, measure latency p50/p95/p99.

Running a benchmark (recipe):
1. Reserve perf-capacity pool (perf-n1-usw2) with identical GPU type as production.
2. Deploy the candidate runtime binary and model bundle.
3. Execute: infra/perf-runner --config perf/configs/chat-128.json --target-url http://perf-gateway:8080/generate --duration 30m
4. Collect outputs: traces/run_id.json, kernels/run_id.kprof, gpu/run_id.csv, summary/run_id-summary.json
5. Compare to baseline with perf-compare tool: perf/tools/perf-compare --baseline b123 --candidate run_id

Acceptance criteria for changes:
- No regression > 5% in p95 latency for short prompts compared to baseline.
- Token throughput should be within +/- 7% of baseline for comparable cost tier.
- GPU memory overhead increase must be < 4% unless justified by quality gains.

## 5) Release notes & upgrade checklist (summary)

Purpose: ensure runtime and kernel changes roll out safely.

Release quick-summary (example for v2.14.0):
- Highlights: improved fused attention kernel for fp16 leading to 18% p95 improvement on chat-128 workloads.
- Breaking changes: kernel ABI change requires rebuild of vendor optimized-kernels (see vendor/kernel-table v1.3).
- Rollout plan: staged rollout across Dedicated pools with 10% canary -> 50% -> 100% over 48h with metrics gates.

Upgrade checklist (pre-rollout):
1. Confirm perf-suite baselines and no regressions in perf-compare.
2. Update kernel-table and artifact storage (s3://redwood-kernels/v2.14.0).
3. Notify SRE & oncall (email + #runtime-release).
4. Create canary config and define gates: p95 latency, error-rate, GPU OOMs.
5. Run smoke tests against canary pool for 6 hours.
6. Proceed with expansion if gates pass.

Gate thresholds (example):
- p95 latency regression > 5% -> fail
- request error rate increase > 0.2% absolute -> fail
- GPU OOM events during canary -> fail and rollback immediately

## 6) Known issues and mitigations

Current notable issues (triaged):
1) Intermittent p99 spikes on long-seq workloads (investigation ongoing)
- Symptom: occasional > 2s p99 for seq_len > 1024 when mixed with short-turn traffic.
- Mitigation: set sequence_length_isolation=true for affected pools.
- Owner: runtime/perf team.

2) Kernel selection fallback can increase latency when optimized kernel not found
- Mitigation: update kernel-table to add entries for common seq_len buckets; enable dynamic JIT for rarely-used kernels.
- Owner: runtime/kernel team.

3) Memory leak in worker after many model load/unload cycles (fixed in v2.13.7 but watch for regressions)
- Mitigation: enforce process recycle via restart window 24h in autoscaler until backport is verified.

For a full, versioned list see: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/known-issues-index (internal link).

## 7) Runtime runbooks (incidents, scaling, rollbacks)

A. High p95 latency (sudden regression)
1. Triage: Check dashboard for p95/p99, token throughput, queue depth and GPU metrics.
2. Identify scope: single pool vs global. Check recent deploys (last 2 hours) using deploy metadata.
3. If deploy in last 2 hours: rollback canary to previous version following rollback playbook (steps below).
4. If no deploy: run profiler on representative worker and capture kernel trace.
5. Temporary mitigation: enable per-request rate-limit or route heavy traffic to lower-latency pool.
6. Postmortem: attach perf artifacts and timeline, assign owner.

Rollback playbook (safe rollback):
1. Pause rollout in console.
2. Set routing policy to prefer previous model/runtime variant for 100% of new requests in affected region.
3. Recycle affected workers gracefully: drain -> stop -> start with previous image.
4. Monitor for 2x the SLO window (e.g., 48 hours) before reattempting upgrade.

B. GPU OOMs / memory pressure
1. Identify process with OOM -> collect dmesg and runtime logs.
2. If transient (single worker), drain and restart worker.
3. If widespread: reduce max_batch_size and enforce seq_len isolation policy.
4. Open urgent PR to revert change that introduced memory increase if correlated.

C. Degraded throughput (tokens/sec drop)
1. Verify autoscaler behavior and reserved capacity.
2. Check for kernel regressions via perf-compare and microbenchmarks.
3. If autoscaling misconfiguration, adjust capacity policy and warm pools.
